analysis: The target is not defined by language tuition in isolation. Both languages underpin original-text analysis and specialist research in poetry, ancient historiography, inscriptions and papyri. Greek and Roman history and material culture and ancient philosophy are integrated with those skills. The ordinary route contains 80 EC of named proficiency, reading and Greek/Latin research seminars, plus 15 EC of poetry, historiography and epigraphy dependent on the first-year two-language sequence. The 10 EC thesis is field-specific. The 30 EC minor permits breadth after that foundation.

The strongest UCR palette makes a genuine classical inquiry attempt. Greek Archaeology and Heritage & Ancient Democracy are direct and sustained contributions. World Myth & Literature uses classical epic, tragedy and Ovid in comparative and reception contexts, and Rhetorical Communication substantively teaches Greek and Roman theory. World Archaeology and History of Empires develop material and historical inquiry across wider settings. Great Literary Works, Western Philosophy, Political Philosophy and Philosophy of Emotion offer substantive ancient content in larger programmes. Replacing unavailable Rhetoric in Action with Philosophy of Emotion strengthens the ancient-philosophy strand. The workbook supports both six-term palettes, so the assessment is independent of the original term conflict.

The literature and archaeology palette broadens into film adaptation, early media, general literary criticism, Western art, Renaissance art, public communication and modern historical methods. Those courses offer real methods and some reception opportunities, but do not sustain advanced Greek and Roman textual, material and historical research together. The democracy and political traditions palette begins with Greek evidence, classical political thought and myth. Its depth is in contemporary or later comparative politics, constitutional law, human rights, international law and conflict. It would be coherent as a politics and history programme, with a substantial classical foundation, but it does not provide a sustained response to Groningen Classics. No course-code count or degree-equivalence requirement was applied.

Additional workbook leads included Life & Travel Writing, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Ethics, Philosophy of Mind, Free Will, Time & the Self, African Art & Heritage and Rhetoric in Action. None supplies the missing ancient literary, historical or material progression. The Renaissance Mediterranean and Writing Art’s Histories receive full consideration for visual and reception work within their actual scope. The American Century course is valuable historical research in another period. Modern persuasion and rhetorical performance do not constitute original-text commentary.

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.text:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century.


Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants.


This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
